title: Sales Questions
summary: 15 real sales interview questions — from losing a deal to going dark on a champion — with the frameworks reps who actually carry a number use to answer them.

sections.heading: "Walk me through your sales process, start to finish."
sections.body:
This is the question that separates reps who can talk about selling from reps who actually sell on repeat. The interviewer isn't asking for a generic funnel — "prospect, qualify, demo, close" — they're checking whether you run a repeatable, disciplined process or whether every deal is a fire drill.

Structure your answer around your own numbers, not theory:
- Sourcing: how deals actually enter your pipeline (outbound sequence, inbound MQL, partner referral, expansion motion) and roughly what share comes from each
- Qualification: the specific framework you use (MEDDIC, MEDDPICC, Command of the Message, BANT) and how you apply it — not just the acronym
- Discovery: how you uncover the business pain and quantify it, not just confirm interest
- Proof/validation: demo, pilot, business case, or ROI model — whichever your deal size actually requires
- Commercial close: how you handle pricing conversations, procurement, and legal
- Handoff: what happens after signature (to CS, onboarding, or renewals)

Name your actual cycle length and close rate at each stage if you can ("about a 45-day average cycle, roughly 25% of qualified opportunities close"). A candidate who says "I use MEDDIC" and then can't explain how they identify the Economic Buyer on a specific deal gets caught immediately — be ready to attach a real example to at least two stages.

Common mistake: reciting a process you read in a sales book instead of the one you actually run. Interviewers who sell for a living can tell the difference in one follow-up question.

sections.heading: "Tell me about a time you lost a big deal. What happened?"
sections.body:
Do not spin this into a secret win ("but we actually learned so much!") — that reads as dodging accountability, which is the opposite of what this question is testing for.

Pick a real, specific loss with real numbers: deal size, stage it died at, and who beat you (competitor, status quo/"no decision," or internal budget freeze). Then walk the actual mechanics:
- What the signal was that you missed or ignored (single-threaded on one champion, no confirmed Economic Buyer, no clear compelling event, or you were competing against a relationship the incumbent had that you didn't know about)
- The moment you realized it was slipping, and what you tried
- What you'd do differently with the qualification lens you have now

Good example shape: "I had a $140K ACV deal with a mid-market logistics company. I was tight with the ops director, my champion, but I never got in front of the CFO who controlled the budget line. At the 11th hour, the CFO killed it to fund a different initiative — my champion never saw it coming either. Now I treat 'who signs the check and have I met them' as a hard gate before I call anything Commit in my forecast."

Key point interviewers are grading: do you do an honest post-mortem, and did it change your behavior on the next deal — not just your mood.

sections.heading: "A prospect says, 'We just don't have budget for this right now.' How do you respond?"
sections.body:
First move: figure out which objection you're actually facing, because "no budget" means three different things —
- Reflexive brush-off early in the call, before you've earned the right to talk money
- Real constraint: the money genuinely isn't allocated this fiscal year
- Soft no: they don't see enough value to fight for the budget internally

Ask directly rather than guessing: "Is this a matter of the budget not existing at all this year, or that this specific initiative isn't the one it's earmarked for yet?" The answer changes your whole next move.

If it's a genuine timing issue, don't disappear — find out when the next budget cycle opens and get a specific commitment to revisit ("Let's put a placeholder on your calendar for October when next year's budget locks, and I'll send you a one-pager you can use internally before then"). If it's really a value gap, go back to the cost of inaction: what is the problem costing them per month by not solving it, and does that number make the "no budget" position hold up when a decision-maker sees it in writing.

Late in a cycle, "no budget" often means "convince me it's worth reallocating from something else" — that's a negotiation, not a dead end, and treating it like a hard no is the mistake weaker reps make.

sections.heading: "Walk me through how you qualify a lead."
sections.body:
Name your framework explicitly and then prove you actually use it with an example — most candidates can recite the acronym and stop there.

If you use MEDDIC/MEDDPICC, be ready to define each letter in one line and attach a real deal to at least three of them: Metrics (the quantified business pain), Economic Buyer (who actually signs), Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Identify Pain (the "why now"), Champion, and in MEDDPICC, Paper Process and Competition.

Concrete answer shape: "I run MEDDIC on every opportunity past first call. On my last renewal-at-risk deal, I had a strong Champion and clear Metrics — they were losing about 8 hours a week to manual reconciliation — but no confirmed Economic Buyer. I flagged it in my pipeline review as a 'Champion only' deal, which meant I didn't advance my forecast stage until I'd gotten a meeting with their VP of Finance."

Make the point that qualification isn't a one-time gate at the top of the funnel — you re-qualify as new information comes in (a stakeholder leaves, a budget freeze hits, a champion gets promoted). A lead that was qualified in week one can become unqualified in week four, and good reps catch that instead of dragging dead opportunities through the pipeline until forecast day.

sections.heading: "Tell me about the biggest deal you've ever closed."
sections.body:
Lead with the number, then tell the story of the one or two moves that actually got it done — not a full chronological retelling of every call.

Frame it as: size and context (ACV, industry, why it was hard), the specific obstacle that could have killed it, the action you took, and the quantified result — including what happened after signature if you know it (expansion, renewal, reference).

Example shape: "My largest deal was $210K ACV with a regional healthcare group. It stalled for six weeks because my champion, a director of ops, couldn't get executive sponsorship — the VP kept declining meetings. I asked my champion what the VP was measured on that quarter, found out it was reducing patient no-show rates, and rebuilt the business case around that single metric instead of our general pitch. That got us fifteen minutes with the VP, and we closed three weeks later. It expanded to $340K the following year when they rolled it out to two more facilities."

What this is testing: whether you can identify the actual blocker (not "they were slow to decide") and describe a specific, replicable action — reframing around a stakeholder's own metric, getting a second-level intro, building a business case — rather than crediting persistence or luck.

sections.heading: "How do you handle rejection, or a string of losses?"
sections.body:
Skip the inspirational-poster answer ("I stay positive!"). Interviewers who've carried a quota want to hear a concrete routine, because sales is a game of ratios and a slump is a data problem before it's a mindset problem.

Describe something specific and repeatable:
- A weekly personal pipeline review where you look at loss reasons by pattern, not just individually
- Pulling call recordings from your last several losses to check for a repeated point where deals stall
- Asking your manager or a peer for a blunt read on one recent loss, not a general "how am I doing"
- Running actual win/loss conversations with prospects who didn't buy, when you can get them on the phone

Then attach a real example of a slump and the specific fix: "I lost four deals in a six-week stretch last year. When I pulled the call recordings, three of the four lost momentum right after I introduced pricing — I was leading with the number before I'd built enough value. I restructured my discovery calls to spend more time quantifying the cost of their current problem before any pricing conversation, and win rate on the next dozen opportunities went up noticeably."

The point: you treat rejection as a pattern to diagnose, not a mood to push through.

sections.heading: "Tell me about selling to a difficult or skeptical stakeholder."
sections.body:
Be specific about who and why — "difficult" almost always means one of a few things: a technical evaluator who thinks you're oversimplifying, a security/legal reviewer whose job is to find reasons to say no, a budget holder who's been burned by a vendor before, or a stakeholder who was happy with the status quo and views you as extra work.

Name which one it was and adapt-in-real-time detail: what did they actually push back on, and what did you change about your approach — not your product, your approach — to address it.

Example shape: "I was selling to a CISO who kept redirecting every call to data residency and breach history instead of the business case my champion cared about. Rather than keep pitching value, I brought our solutions engineer onto the next call specifically to walk through our SOC 2 report and data handling architecture, and let the CISO run that conversation instead of steering it myself. Once that box was checked, he stopped blocking and the deal moved."

The lesson to make explicit: you met the stakeholder in their own language and metrics instead of repeating your standard deck at them louder. That adaptability — not persistence — is what the question is actually probing.

sections.heading: "How do you approach a prospect who's already happy with a competitor?"
sections.body:
Don't lead with attacking the incumbent — it reads as insecure and prospects tune it out fast. The real skill is finding the specific wedge: a gap in what the incumbent delivers, a timing event (renewal, contract expiration, a champion change), or a frustration the prospect hasn't voiced loudly yet.

Concrete moves to describe:
- Ask what's working and what's frustrating about the current tool separately — most people will volunteer the frustration once asked directly and specifically, even if they wouldn't lead with it
- Find out the renewal date early; timing a real conversation 60-90 days before renewal is far more productive than pitching mid-contract with no urgency
- Identify who champions the incumbent internally versus who's quietly unhappy — a new stakeholder (new VP, new team lead) is often your actual opening

Example: "I displaced an incumbent at a mid-size retailer by timing outreach for 90 days before their renewal and asking their ops manager directly what she'd change if she could. She mentioned their current tool's support SLA was a constant headache — a pain point that never showed up in their public reviews. I built the whole pitch around response-time guarantees instead of feature parity, and that specific gap is what got us the pilot."

Point to land: incumbency isn't beaten with a better feature list, it's beaten with a specific, named pain the current vendor isn't solving.

sections.heading: "Tell me about a time you missed quota. What did you do?"
sections.body:
Give the actual number — "78% of quota in Q3," not "I had a tough quarter." Vague answers here read as either dishonest or like you never actually tracked your own performance closely enough to know.

Then do a real root-cause, and be precise about which part of the funnel broke, because "missed quota" can mean completely different problems:
- Top-of-funnel: not enough qualified pipeline generated (a coverage-ratio problem)
- Mid-funnel: pipeline stalled or slipped past forecasted close dates
- Late-funnel: deals were reaching the finish line and dying there (pricing, competition, procurement)

Say which one it was for you, specifically: "My pipeline coverage was only about 2x quota that quarter instead of the 3.5-4x I need historically to hit number — the shortfall was top-of-funnel, not my close rate, which was actually fine on what I had." Then name the concrete fix you made — increased outbound volume, added a new lead source, changed your target account list — and what happened the following quarter as a result.

What this answer needs to avoid: blaming marketing, the economy, or your territory in a way that has no counterpart action you took. A miss with no diagnosis and no fix is a red flag; a miss with a clear root cause and a next-quarter recovery is a normal, credible sales story.

sections.heading: "How do you prioritize your pipeline when you have too many accounts to work well?"
sections.body:
The tell-tale weak answer here is "I just work my biggest deals first" with no actual system. Give a real triage method.

Talk through the inputs you actually weigh:
- Pipeline coverage ratio against quota (most orgs need roughly 3-4x quota in pipeline to reliably hit number — know your own number)
- MEDDIC/qualification completeness — a deal missing two or more criteria (no Economic Buyer confirmed, no compelling event) gets deprioritized or actively disqualified, not just ignored
- Recency of engagement — a "hot" deal that's gone quiet for three weeks needs attention before a smaller, newly-engaged one
- Deal size weighted by realistic probability, not just logo size — a large logo with a weak champion and no budget confirmed is often lower priority than it looks

Concrete example: "When my book got to around 40 open opportunities, I started a weekly Monday triage where I ran every deal against my MEDDIC checklist. Anything missing an Economic Buyer or a compelling event after being open more than 30 days got moved to a nurture cadence instead of active pursuit — that freed up roughly a third of my week to focus on the dozen deals that were actually qualified and moving."

The point: prioritization by deal size alone is amateur; prioritization by qualification strength plus size is what experienced reps actually do.

sections.heading: "Walk me through how you handle procurement and legal at the end of a deal."
sections.body:
The mistake this question is fishing for: reps who treat procurement/legal/security as a surprise that shows up at the finish line instead of a track they've been running in parallel the whole time.

Describe getting these workstreams started early, not after verbal agreement:
- Ask about the prospect's procurement and security review process during discovery, not after the demo — "what does approval typically look like on your end once a decision is made?"
- Have your standard security documentation (SOC 2 report, DPA template, standard MSA redlines) ready to send the moment it's requested, not scrambled together under deadline pressure
- Loop in your own deal desk or legal early on anything non-standard, so you're not negotiating terms live on a call you're not authorized to agree to
- Keep your champion engaged during the "boring middle" — paperwork stretches are where deals quietly die because nobody's driving urgency

Example: "On a deal that had to close by quarter-end, I knew from discovery that their security team required a completed vendor questionnaire before any contract review started. I had our SOC 2 report and a filled-out standard questionnaire ready to send the day pricing was verbally agreed, instead of waiting for them to ask — that alone probably saved a week we didn't have."

This is a process-discipline question disguised as a procurement question — answer it that way.

sections.heading: "Tell me about a time you had to multi-thread a deal to get it done."
sections.body:
Define the term in passing so your answer is self-contained, then get straight to the specific mechanics of how you did it — that's what's actually being tested.

Multi-threading means building relationships with more than one stakeholder so the deal doesn't die if your one contact goes quiet, changes jobs, or turns out not to have real authority. Single-threaded deals are fragile — champions get reorganized, leave the company, or simply can't sell internally as well as you'd hoped.

Concrete example: "I had a champion, a marketing ops manager, who was enthusiastic but had no budget authority and admitted she'd struggle to sell it up to her VP. Instead of coaching her to pitch her boss alone, I asked her to set up a 20-minute business review framed around the VP's own quarterly goal — reducing campaign turnaround time — and I ran that meeting jointly with her instead of behind her. That got the VP directly invested, and when my original champion went on leave two weeks before close, the deal didn't stall because the VP was already bought in independently."

Name the mechanism explicitly in your close: multi-threading isn't about meeting more people for its own sake, it's about making sure at least one relationship with real authority survives any single point of failure.

sections.heading: "How do you forecast your pipeline, and how accurate are your forecasts?"
sections.body:
Sales managers ask this because inaccurate forecasting — in either direction — creates real problems for the business, and they're checking whether you understand that or just report optimistic numbers upward.

Describe your actual categories and the criteria for each, not just labels:
- Commit: verbal agreement on price and scope, a signed or agreed mutual close plan, budget confirmed by the Economic Buyer, and a realistic path through procurement before period end
- Best case: strong momentum but missing one hard criterion above (usually budget confirmation or a firm close date)
- Pipeline/upside: everything else that's genuinely active

Give a real accuracy number if you have one: "I've forecasted within about 90% of actual for the last three quarters running." If you don't have that exact figure, describe the discipline instead: a weekly 1:1 pipeline review with your manager where every Commit deal has to survive specific questions before it counts.

Address both failure modes honestly, because interviewers know both happen: sandbagging (holding deals out of Commit that you're actually confident in, to look conservative) and happy-ears (calling something Commit because you want it to close, not because the criteria are met). Say plainly that you correct for the second one especially — it's the one that damages trust with your manager fastest when a "Commit" deal slips.

sections.heading: "What do you do when your champion goes quiet mid-deal?"
sections.body:
The weak answer is "I follow up a few more times." Show a specific escalation sequence instead.

Steps worth naming in order:
- Vary the channel — a call after three unanswered emails, then a LinkedIn message, rather than sending the same email a fourth time
- Check for a job change — a champion going dark is very often a champion who left or got reassigned; a quick LinkedIn check can save weeks of guessing
- Re-engage with something of specific value, not just "checking in" — a relevant case study, a real deadline (end-of-quarter pricing, a pending price increase), or new information that changes their calculus
- Reach a secondary contact if you built one — this is exactly why multi-threading earlier in the deal matters; if your champion is your only path, you have no fallback

Example: "My champion went quiet for about two weeks after we'd verbally agreed on scope. After the second unanswered email, I called instead, then checked LinkedIn and saw she'd moved to a new role internally — she just hadn't looped anyone in yet. I asked her directly who'd taken over the initiative, got introduced to her replacement, and re-ran a condensed version of the business case with the new stakeholder. It added three weeks to the cycle but the deal closed."

The point to land explicitly: silence is information, not just an inconvenience — treat it as a signal to investigate, not just a reason to email again.

sections.heading: "Tell me about a time you expanded or upsold an existing account."
sections.body:
Give real before-and-after numbers — this question is checking whether you think about accounts as ongoing relationships with growth potential, or as one-time transactions you move on from after signature.

Name the actual expansion signal you spotted: usage data showing they'd hit a plan limit, a new department discovering the tool organically, a renewal conversation surfacing a new use case, or a champion getting promoted into a role with a bigger budget and bringing you with them.

Example: "An account I'd closed at $40K ACV for one team started showing usage patterns that suggested a second department was using it informally through shared logins. I flagged it with my champion instead of ignoring it, framed it as a compliance and reporting gap rather than a violation, and proposed a formal expansion covering both teams with proper seat licensing. It grew the account to $95K ACV at the next renewal, and gave me a second internal champion in the process."

If you work with a Customer Success or Account Management team, say so and describe the handoff specifically — how you stay looped in on health signals without stepping on their relationship, since a hoarding answer ("I just kept managing the whole relationship myself") can read as a red flag in orgs with a real CS motion.

The core point: expansion comes from watching for signals proactively, not waiting for the renewal date to ask "want to buy more?"
